title: What are nullable reference types in C#?
description: Compiler-null-safety annotations: how NRT changes the contract, ? and !, nullability warnings, and migrating legacy code.

data.text: **Question:** What are nullable reference types in C#?

Nullable reference types (C# 8+, enabled with `#nullable enable`) are a **compile-time null-safety system** — annotations the compiler uses to warn about possible `NullReferenceException`s before they run. `string` means 'never null by contract' and generates warnings on possible nulls; `string?` means 'null is part of the value' and requires a null check before dereferencing. It is **not runtime enforcement**: no exception is thrown automatically, no type changes at runtime — it's a disciplined contract between producers and consumers that turns a whole class of runtime crashes into build warnings.

**The mechanics:**
- `#nullable enable` per file, project-wide via `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` in the csproj (default for new .NET projects)
- `string name` — contract: never null. Assigning null warns (CS8600); dereferencing a maybe-null warns (CS8602)
- `string? name` — null is expected. Dereferencing without a check warns; the compiler tracks flow and **learns from your checks**: `if (name is not null) name.Trim()` — no warning
- `null!` (null-forgiving) — 'I know this is null but stop warning' — for initialization patterns where the framework fills it later (EF navigation properties, constructor-injected services)
- Attributes express intent in APIs: `[NotNullWhen(true)]`, `[MaybeNull]`, `[AllowNull]`, `[MemberNotNull]` — they teach the compiler about out-params and guards
- Value types: `int?` was always nullable; NRT is specifically about **reference types**

**What it changes in practice:**
- Warnings (CS86xx), not errors — you choose when to escalate with `<TreatWarningsAsErrors>`
- Flow analysis is per-variable and path-sensitive — branches teach the compiler state
- Public API nullability becomes part of the contract: consumers of your library see warnings based on your annotations
- Doesn't detect every NRE: null can flow through reflection, uninitialized fields, or `!`-suppressed code

**Migrating legacy code:**
- Enable per-project gradually: start with `<Nullable>annotations</Nullable>` (annotate but don't warn), then flip to `enable`
- Silence hot spots with `#nullable disable` around noisy generated files, then re-enable file by file
- Don't sprinkle `!` to go green — that just moves the NullReferenceException runtime without fixing the contract
- Design fixes beat annotation fixes: TryGet patterns (`bool TryParse(string, out string? result)`), constructor guarantees, and non-null defaults remove the nulls instead of describing them

data.title: Flow analysis, guards, and API attributes
Annotations are a contract, not a runtime feature
data.text: At runtime, `string` and `string?` are the same type — nothing is checked and nothing throws. The value is entirely in the compile-time warnings and in what your API communicates to consumers. Treat nullability annotations like types on your public surface: accurate annotations make callers safe by construction; dishonest ones (`null!` everywhere) are worse than no annotations at all.

Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing NRT is compile-time only — warnings, not runtime checks
- Flow analysis: the compiler learns from null checks and guard clauses
- Practical tools: `?`, `null!`, `[NotNullWhen]`, Try-patterns
- Honest limits: reflection, generated code, and `!` abuse fall outside the system

items: Suppressing every warning with ! to get a green build — the NREs just move to runtime
Marking a property string (non-null) that your deserializer frequently leaves null
Forgetting that flow analysis is per-variable — calling a method that returns the same value doesn't inherit the proof
Enabling NRT project-wide in a legacy codebase in one PR — enable in annotations mode first
Assuming NRT guarantees no NullReferenceException — unannotated code and reflection bypass it
Mixing annotated and unannotated assemblies without checking how warnings surface at boundaries
What does null! actually do — does it change anything at runtime?
How do you annotate an out parameter so callers aren't warned when you return false?
How would you migrate a 5-year-old codebase to nullable enable without stopping feature work?
What's the difference between `string?` and a nullable value type like `int?`?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: NRT = compile-time null-safety via annotations and flow analysis
`string` = never null by contract; `string?` = null is expected
The compiler learns from is-null checks; guards + [NotNullWhen] extend that to APIs
Warnings, not errors or runtime checks — null! suppresses, doesn't fix
Migrate gradually: annotations mode first, then enable, then treat warnings as errors
data.takeaway: Nullable reference types let you prove null-handling at compile time — annotate honestly, let flow analysis do the work, and design nulls out of the API instead of annotating around them.
